media:group.media:description: Join me on this emotional and eye-opening journey as I share my personal experience of living with ALS for the past year. If you or someone you know is going through a similar experience, I hope that my story can provide some comfort, support, and inspiration. So, let's take this journey together and raise awareness about ALS, and let's work towards finding a cure for this devastating disease. 💛

entry.title: This Is What I Want My Wife to Hear After I’m Gone | ALS Love Letter

media:group.media:title: This Is What I Want My Wife to Hear After I’m Gone | ALS Love Letter
media:group.media:description:
If you are living with ALS, loving someone with ALS, or grieving a future you never asked for, this video is for you.
This is a deeply personal love letter to my wife, Denise. I recorded it knowing that one day she may watch it after I am gone. ALS, also known as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Lou Gehrig’s disease, and motor neuron disease (MND), has a way of forcing conversations no one is ever ready to have. This video is one of those conversations.
I am living with ALS, a progressive neurodegenerative disease that affects motor neurons and slowly takes away physical function. ALS is terminal. There is no cure. It changes your body, your future, and the way you love. But it does not erase who you are, and it does not erase love.
This video is not about fear. It is not about statistics. It is not about timelines.
It is about gratitude, marriage, devotion, and the kind of love that remains even when a disease tries to take everything else.
If you or someone you love has been diagnosed with ALS, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Lou Gehrig’s disease, or motor neuron disease (MND), you know the quiet weight that comes with it. The unspoken thoughts. The late nights. The moments where joy and grief exist in the same breath. This video is meant to speak into that space.
Caregivers, spouses, partners, and family members often carry more than they let on. This is for you too. Loving someone with ALS means learning how to hold on and let go at the same time. It means showing up even when the future feels unfair. It means loving fiercely in the present.
I wanted to leave something behind that wasn’t medical updates or explanations of ALS symptoms, progression, or treatments. I wanted to leave my wife something timeless. Something human. Something that says this life mattered, this love mattered, and you did everything right.
If you are here because you searched for ALS videos, ALS diagnosis stories, living with ALS, ALS caregiver support, terminal illness journeys, or motor neuron disease awareness, I hope you feel seen. I hope you feel less alone. And I hope this reminds you that even in the middle of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, love still wins.
This channel exists to document life with ALS honestly. The hard days. The meaningful moments. The gratitude. The grief. And the choice to keep finding joy anyway.
If this video resonates with you, consider subscribing. You are not alone in this journey.
Go find some joy.

entry.title: When Your ALS Doctor Says 2–5 Years…

media:group.media:title: When Your ALS Doctor Says 2–5 Years…
media:group.media:description:
I was told I have 2–5 years to live. This is what I’m choosing to do with every single minute that remains.
When an ALS doctor gives you a timeline, it changes everything. It rearranges your priorities, strips away the noise, and forces you to decide how you want to live. I could live in fear. I could count the days. Or I could choose gratitude, presence, and joy, even while living with ALS.
I’m living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as ALS disease, Lou Gehrig’s disease, and motor neuron disease (MND). It’s a terminal illness that slowly takes away muscle function, independence, and certainty. But it does not take away purpose. It does not take away love. And it does not get to decide how I show up.
This video is for anyone who has received a life-altering diagnosis. It’s for ALS patients, caregivers, family members, loved ones, and friends trying to understand what this disease really feels like. It’s for those navigating chronic illness, terminal illness, neurodegenerative disease, and the fear that comes with an uncertain future.
Living with ALS means learning to let go of the life you imagined while fiercely holding onto what still matters. It means redefining strength, finding joy in small moments, and choosing to live fully instead of waiting for someday.
If you or someone you love is affected by ALS, MND, or another terminal diagnosis, know this: your story is still being written. Your life still has meaning. And joy is still possible, even here.
This is how I’m choosing to live with ALS. One minute at a time. With gratitude. With intention. With joy

entry.title: December Changed Me More Than Expected (ALS Update)

media:group.media:title: December Changed Me More Than Expected (ALS Update)
media:group.media:description:
This December ALS update is one of the most honest ones I’ve shared… because this month has changed me more than I expected. If you’re living with ALS, caring for someone with ALS, or trying to understand what amyotrophic lateral sclerosis actually feels like day to day, I hope this video finds you.
ALS — also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease or motor neuron disease (MND) — doesn’t follow a straight line. Some months feel manageable. Some months hit harder. December has been a mix of both. There’s been more weakness in places I used to rely on, more fatigue, more moments where I’ve had to adjust how I do things or ask for help. That part is never easy.
But there’s also been gratitude. There’s been joy. There’s been the work of accepting what’s changing while still being myself inside all of it. And that’s what this update is really about: how to hold the reality of ALS progression and still find ways to stay hopeful, grounded, and connected.
If you’re searching for stories about ALS, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Lou Gehrig’s disease, or MND because you or someone you love has been affected, you’re in the right place. I share these updates to give a real look at what this disease does, but also to remind people that joy doesn’t disappear — it just changes shape.
December has brought harder symptoms, slower days, and some emotional moments… but it’s also brought community, support, and small wins that mean everything. And as we head into a new year, that’s what I’m choosing to hold on to.
If this update resonates with you, share it with someone who needs it. Drop a comment with one small thing that brought you joy this month — I love reading those. And to everyone living with ALS or caring for someone with a terminal neurological disease: you are not alone. We’re in this together.
Go find some joy today. Even in December. Especially in December.

entry.title: My 2-Year Journey with ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis) — From Pre-Diagnosis to Silent Voice

media:group.media:title: My 2-Year Journey with ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis) — From Pre-Diagnosis to Silent Voice
media:group.media:description:
You don’t want to miss this: a raw, unfiltered look at two years of progression with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also called Lou Gehrig’s disease, motor neuron disease (MND), Charcot’s disease.
Two days before I was diagnosed. One year later. And today, unable to speak. This video shows the physical and emotional reality of living with ALS/MND – the good moments, the hardest moments, the truth no filter.
I started with hope and movement. A year in I was still pushing, still fighting. Today the voice is gone, but the story remains. I share this so others affected by ALS, motor neuron disease, Lou Gehrig’s disease, Charcot’s disease – and their families, friends, caregivers – see someone who’s walking (well, wheeling) the same path. You’re not alone.
What you’ll see in this video:
Clip from just before diagnosis – full mobility, everyday routine.
One-year update – changes in strength, speech, movement.
Today – the body has changed, speech lost, but spirit still here.
My reflections on fear, hope, love, community, and finding joy despite ALS/MND.
Why I’m sharing this:
To raise awareness of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), motor neuron disease (MND), Lou Gehrig’s disease. Wikipedia +2 The ALS Association +2
To show progression visually so others understand how quickly and unevenly ALS/MND can change life. The ALS Association +1
To connect with families, caregivers, friends and people living with ALS/MND — your story matters.
To say: even when you lose your voice, your story still has power.
Who this is for:
Anyone recently diagnosed with ALS, motor neuron disease (MND), Charcot’s disease, Lou Gehrig’s disease.
Family members, spouses, caregivers trying to understand what’s ahead.
Friends who want to support someone with ALS/MND.
Advocates, researchers, viewers curious about what life looks like with this neurological disease.
Important keywords you’ll hear in the video: ALS, MND, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Lou Gehrig’s disease, Charcot’s disease, motor neuron disease, progressive neurodegenerative disease, wheelchair life, disability, voice lost, communication device.
Warning / note: Some parts are hard to watch. Some may trigger emotional responses. But I believe in truth. I believe in showing life—not just the highlight reel—with ALS/MND.
What I hope you’ll do after watching:
Share this video if you know someone impacted by ALS/MND.
Comment your story below — whether you have ALS/MND, are a caregiver, or know someone. Let’s build community.
Hit subscribe if you’ll follow this journey onward — I’ll continue documenting, showing what it really means to live with ALS.
Thank you: to my wife, daughter, her boyfriend, friends, family; to all the caregivers, therapists, medical professionals; and to everyone fighting or supporting someone with ALS/MND. We see you, we value you.
Final thought: Life with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) or motor neuron disease (MND) may change everything — movement, speech, independence — but it does not erase the person, the love, the story. If you or someone you know has been touched by ALS/Lou Gehrig’s disease/Charcot’s disease — this one is for you.

entry.title: I Thought ALS Was The End But I Was Wrong

media:group.media:title: I Thought ALS Was The End But I Was Wrong
media:group.media:description:
Two years after being diagnosed with ALS, I’m sharing the truth about how this disease has changed my life — and the surprising ways it’s deepened my gratitude, my purpose, and my joy.
This is the most honest and emotional video I’ve ever made. I filmed myself reacting to my own ElevenLabs voiceover as I reflect on what these two years have actually looked like — not just the physical decline, but the moments that kept me going: walking my daughter Kendall down the aisle, time with my wife Denise, and discovering just how many kind people exist in the world.
ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) — also called Lou Gehrig’s disease, motor neuron disease (MND), neuromuscular disease, or progressive muscle atrophy — has taken so much from me. I had to retire from teaching. I rely on other people for everything now. My muscles are weakening, my independence is shrinking, and every day brings some new challenge.
But these two years have also shown me something unexpected: humanity is beautiful. People are good. Community is powerful. And joy is still possible… even here.
In this video, I talk about:
What I’ve learned since being diagnosed with ALS
How ALS forced me to retire from teaching after 17 years
What it feels like to rely completely on others
The emotional impact on my family — especially Denise
The highlight of my year: walking my daughter down the aisle
How my perspective on life has completely changed
Why “Go Find Some Joy” isn’t just a slogan — it’s survival
Advice for anyone newly diagnosed with ALS
Why kindness matters more now than ever
If you or someone you love is affected by ALS, I hope this video reaches you at the right moment. Whether you're dealing with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, MND, Lou Gehrig’s disease, upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, neurodegenerative disease, paralysis, progressive muscle weakness, or you’re just here to understand what this journey looks like — you’re not alone.
My mission is simple: Tell the truth. Spread awareness. And help people find joy even in the hardest places.
If you want to support my journey, my GoFundMe link is below. Every donation helps with caregiving costs, accessibility devices, medical needs, and giving my family a little more time and peace during a brutal disease.
💙 GoFundMe: www.gofindsomejoy.com
(Even if you can’t give, just sharing the link means everything.)
✨ If you're newly diagnosed:
Your life is not over. Yes, ALS is devastating. Yes, it will change everything. But there is still love. Still joy. Still purpose. Don’t wait for life to be perfect. Go find some joy.
❤️ Thank You
To everyone who has watched, commented, donated, prayed, or messaged me… you’ve made these two years easier than they should’ve been. My family and I feel your love every day.
Thank you for being part of this journey. Thank you for helping me keep going. And thank you for helping me continue to spread hope to others.

entry.title: I Have ALS, But I’m Not Giving Up

media:group.media:title: I Have ALS, But I’m Not Giving Up
media:group.media:description:
What if I told you I can’t change my diagnosis… but I can change the way I live through it? In this video, I share my most honest and unfiltered life and health update since my last vlog. Living with ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis) isn’t easy — but this journey has taught me that joy still exists in the middle of pain.
Since my last update, a lot has changed. I recently had a G-tube placed, and honestly, it’s been one of the best decisions I’ve made. My energy is better, eating is no longer exhausting, and I’m slowly finding a new rhythm. I’m still working on stamina — lots of naps, lots of lying down — but the difference in daily comfort is huge.
That said, ALS doesn’t stop moving. My legs, once my strongest muscle group, have gotten weaker, making transfers more challenging. My clinic appointments feel like data collection sessions — more tests, more decline — not exactly hopeful. There’s still no wheelchair, because insurance is a slow-motion nightmare.
But here’s the thing: even when the body breaks down, life keeps showing up with reasons to smile.
A couple of weeks ago, our backyard turned into a wedding venue when Kendall and Josh said “I do.” It was small, intimate, and perfect. I wasn’t sure I’d live to see that moment back in July, but I did. And now, in just a couple of weeks, my oldest daughter Madison is getting married too. Two weddings. Two miracles. One proud dad.
Between family visits, amazing caregivers, and my wife Denise — my rock, my best friend, my everything — I’m surrounded by love. That’s what keeps me grounded. That’s what keeps me laughing, even through the decline.
I’m also learning to communicate through eye gaze technology — using my eyes to speak. It’s wild and humbling, but I’m determined to become an expert. ALS can take my voice, but it doesn’t get to take my story.
This video isn’t about sadness — it’s about perspective. It’s about learning to live fully while you still can. Because if there’s one thing this disease has taught me, it’s that you don’t have to wait for life to be perfect to find joy in it.
💙 Whether you’re newly diagnosed, a caregiver, a family member, or just someone who stumbled here looking for hope — I see you. You’re not alone in this.
🧭 My mission is simple: help others living with ALS (also known as Lou Gehrig’s Disease or Motor Neuron Disease) find connection, comfort, and courage.
If this story resonates with you, please share it — and if you’d like to help me continue creating these videos and raising awareness, consider donating to my GoFundMe at www.gofindsomejoy.com . Every bit goes toward medical equipment, accessibility, and continuing this journey with dignity and purpose.

entry.title: How I’m Living Joyfully with ALS

media:group.media:title: How I’m Living Joyfully with ALS
media:group.media:description:
I used to love playing catch. The sound of the ball hitting the glove, the feeling of release — simple moments that meant everything. ALS took that part of my life, but it didn’t take my joy.
Now, I sit back and watch my caregiver throw for me. And somehow, that same joy still finds its way in.
ALS changes what you can do — but not what you can feel.
